title: Fresh Garden Salsa
imagePrompt: A rustic bowl holds bright red salsa with a clearly chunky texture — small, distinct cubes of ripe tomato suspended in a thicker, slightly darker-red blended base. Flecks of chopped cilantro and pale translucent onion are visible throughout, along with tiny bits of red and green pepper skin. A few tortilla chips lean into the bowl, one dipped and glistening with clinging salsa, juice pooling faintly where it rests against the bowl's edge.
subtitle: A fresh-tomato, chop-and-blend base you can freely adapt — tune the peppers to whatever heat and flavor you're after.

ingredients.heading: Ingredients
ingredients.note: This is a starting point, not a fixed formula — scale up freely for a big garden haul, and swap peppers per the guide in Step 2 to land the heat and flavor you want.
items: 1 lb fresh tomatoes (about 3 medium or 8–10 Roma/paste tomatoes), cored
2 fresh jalapeños, stemmed (seed for less heat) — see Step 2 for swaps
⅓ cup white onion, roughly chopped (red onion works too)
⅓ cup fresh cilantro, leaves and tender stems
2 cloves garlic
2 tbsp fresh lime juice (about 1 lime)
¾ tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
½ tsp sugar (optional — balances acidity in very tart tomatoes)
¼ tsp ground cumin (optional, for depth)
ingredients.callout: Key tip: Garden tomatoes vary a lot in water content and acidity — taste as you go and adjust salt, lime, and sugar at the end rather than trusting exact amounts.

substitutes: See pepper guide in Step 2 for other heat/flavor options

body.html: A fresh, chunky salsa built from garden tomatoes instead of canned — this version uses a hybrid technique: half the tomatoes get hand-diced and folded in at the end for real chunks, while the rest gets pulsed with the aromatics into a thicker base. That solves the classic blender problem of everything turning into juice.

items: Mise en place — wash the produce, gather the pepper options, measure seasonings, and set up the blender
Pick your peppers using the heat + flavor guide in Step 2
Hand-dice half the tomatoes; rough-chop the rest
Pulse-blend the rough-chopped tomatoes with the aromatics into a base
Fold in the reserved diced tomato for texture, then rest and taste

body.html: This is a template: treat every quantity here as a starting ratio. Scale it up for a big batch, swap in whatever fresh chiles you've got, and adjust to taste at each stage rather than following it exactly.

items: Wash and dry the tomatoes, peppers, cilantro, and lime.
Gather 1 lb tomatoes and the available pepper options; the recipe default is 2 jalapeños.
Measure ⅓ cup onion and ⅓ cup cilantro; peel 2 garlic cloves.
Juice the lime and measure 2 tbsp lime juice, ¾ tsp kosher salt, optional ½ tsp sugar, and optional ¼ tsp cumin.
Set out a blender or food processor, cutting board, sharp knife, and two bowls—one for the hand-diced tomatoes and one for the finished salsa.

body.html: Control the heat: Read the pepper guide next and choose before chopping; use gloves for very hot chiles and avoid touching your face.

slides.title: Pick Your Peppers
slides.checkboxLabel: Choose peppers for your target heat + flavor

body.html: Every fresh chile brings a different heat level and flavor — heat alone isn't the whole story. Use this as a reference for what you've got, from mildest to hottest:

items: Poblano — ~1,000–1,500 SHU. Mild, rich, green-bean-like flavor. Adds body and a slight earthiness with almost no heat.
Jalapeño — ~2,500–8,000 SHU. Bright and grassy with moderate, straightforward heat. This recipe's default — 2 gives a real but manageable kick.
Fresno — ~2,500–10,000 SHU. Similar heat range to jalapeño but fruitier and slightly sweeter, with a crisp texture and vivid red color that flecks nicely through salsa.
Serrano — ~10,000–23,000 SHU. Jalapeño's hotter, grassier sibling. Roughly 1 serrano ≈ 2 jalapeños in heat — swap in for more fire without changing the flavor much.
Cayenne (fresh) — ~30,000–50,000 SHU. Thin-walled with a sharp, clean heat and little fruitiness. Mince fine and add gradually.
Chile de árbol (fresh) — ~15,000–30,000 SHU. Bright, biting heat that builds quickly; a little goes a long way.
Habanero — ~100,000–350,000 SHU. Intense heat with a distinct tropical-fruit aroma. Start with a quarter pepper, seeded and deveined, minced very fine.
Thai bird's eye — ~50,000–100,000 SHU. Small, fast, sharp heat that hits quick and fades. Slice thin, add a little at a time.

body.html: Got an unlabeled pepper from the garden? Judge by size and shape first: small, thin, and pointed usually means hotter (serrano, chile de árbol, bird's eye); wide, thick-walled, or lantern-shaped ranges from very mild (poblano) to blazing (habanero) depending on the variety. Ripe red is typically hotter and sweeter than the same pepper picked green. When unsure, cut a tiny sliver and taste it raw before committing a whole pepper to the batch — you can always blend in more heat, but you can't take it out.

For this batch: the ingredient list assumes 2 jalapeños for a solid, everyday-spicy salsa. Swap 1 jalapeño for 1 serrano to push it hotter, or add a thin sliver of habanero alongside the jalapeños if you want real heat without losing the base flavor.

slides.title: Prep for Texture
slides.checkboxLabel: Hand-dice half the tomatoes; rough-chop the rest

items: Core the tomatoes. Hand-dice half into small, even ¼-inch cubes and set aside — this is what gives the finished salsa real chunks instead of an all-blended texture.
Rough-chop the remaining half into large chunks; this portion goes into the blender.
Rough-chop the onion, garlic, and peppers. Remove pepper seeds and ribs for less heat, or keep some in for more.
Roughly chop the cilantro, stems and all.

body.html: Skip the blender entirely? You can — finely hand-chop everything (peppers, onion, garlic, cilantro) and stir it into the diced tomato instead of blending. That gives you pico de gallo: no liquid base, all texture. The technique below is a middle ground.

slides.title: Build the Base
slides.checkboxLabel: Pulse the rough-chopped tomatoes with the aromatics

items: Add the rough-chopped tomatoes (not the reserved diced half), onion, garlic, cilantro, and peppers to a food processor or blender.
Add the lime juice, salt, sugar, and cumin.
Pulse in short 1–2 second bursts, checking texture between pulses. Stop once it's a thick, slightly chunky puree — not a smooth liquid.
Taste now and adjust heat before folding anything else in — this is the easiest point to add more pepper if it needs it.

body.html: Key tip: Pulse, don't run continuously. A blender left running whips air and liquid into the tomatoes and turns the base watery fast.

slides.title: Fold, Rest & Taste Again
slides.checkboxLabel: Fold in reserved diced tomato, rest, and re-season

items: Fold the reserved hand-diced tomato into the blended base — this is what keeps every bite chunky instead of uniform.
Taste and adjust salt, lime, or heat as needed.
Transfer to a bowl or jar and let it rest 15–20 minutes (in the fridge if you can) — this is the classic restaurant-salsa trick that lets the flavors settle and meld.
Give it a final stir and taste before serving; fresh tomatoes vary batch to batch, so this last check matters more than any exact measurement above.

body.html: Storage: Keeps well covered in the fridge for about 5 days. Fresh-tomato salsa is more watery than canned-tomato versions and won't hold quite as long.
